title: The Rule Wasn’t Broken
author: Stefan Norrvall
summary: Stefan Norrvall challenges the default organisational diagnosis that a failure means someone did not follow the rule. He observes that people often cite constraints that say less than claimed, and that an organisation's library of frameworks, delegations and standards frequently contradicts itself. His proposed first move is the citation test: ask for the actual clause, and until it is produced treat non-compliance as an allegation rather than a diagnosis. He sorts the gaps into three families: practice, where the rule exists but is unreachable; content, where it is silent, unenactable or contradictory; and authority, where it is written in the wrong place or overridden. Each family needs its own fix, and enforcement suits only genuine non-compliance. He closes with three questions for Monday and a call for visible, authorised overrides.
points: The citation test turns an accusation of non-compliance into a testable claim by demanding the specific provision that governed the decision.
Gaps fall into practice, content and authority families, and a fix aimed at the wrong family, especially enforcement, makes things worse.
Contradictory documents are described as a library problem in which each framework makes sense alone but the set assigns the same decision to different owners.
Overrides should be authorised and recorded with a named decider, rationale and expiry, which also turns repeated overrides into diagnostic evidence.
For novel situations guidance should say who decides, within what limits and who arbitrates, rather than trying to specify the work in advance.
quotes: But what people say a constraint requires and what it actually says are often far apart. Ask for the specific wording and you regularly find the design was shaped by assumptions about the rule rather than the rule itself, and that there is more room to move than anyone thought.
Nobody is technical wrong, which is exactly the problem. When people argue about who decides, they are not trading opinions.
It punishes people for failing to follow rules that were missing, impossible, contradictory or nowhere to be found. They learn that the safest move is not to decide.
If a failure is put down to someone breaching a policy, procedure, standard or delegation, ask for the provision, and for why it applied to that decision. Not the spirit of the framework.
The second is more common than most leaders think. The rule is documented but unreachable.
Enforce the rule at the gate and you punish the person with the least power, and nothing changes.
But an override that leaves no record is authority without accountability. If an organisation is serious about accountability, overrides carry a name and an expiry date.
Most of the gaps in this essay are not missing instructions. They are missing answers to who decides.
